1:
The wall stood whole at last, every breach closed, and only the great doors still wanting to their gates — and it is precisely at this moment of near-completion that the enemies of Judah change their tactics from open assault to intrigue. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the cast and the grammar. Sanballat, Tobiah, Geshem the Arabian, and “the rest of our enemies” — by whom, drawing on Nehemiah 4:7, they understand the Ashdodites and other hostile neighbours first named at Nehemiah 2:19 — heard that the work was done. The idiom, they observe, is passive: “it was heard by him,” a construction growing commoner in the later Hebrew of this book. And the clause about the doors is a deliberate parenthesis, limiting what has just been said: the wall was up, yet down to that time the gates still hung without their doors.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the timing as calculated malice. The enemies had good intelligence of how far the work was advanced; reckoning it as good as done, they saw it must be now or never if they were to strike Nehemiah down. They knew him too well guarded to be attacked on the spot, and so resolved to try what the arts of wheedling could do — to get him among them by fair words. Henry catches the hellish subtlety of the proposal: not a meeting in any city, which might have betrayed a design to seize him, but in some village in the lot of Benjamin, under colour of consulting the common interests of their provinces or of cultivating a better understanding. It is probable, he thinks, that Nehemiah had secret intelligence that they meant to imprison or murder him; certainly he knew them too well to trust their fair speech. They spoke friendship and meant a mischief; Nehemiah believed them not.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds two fine observations. First, on the naming: “the Three” — Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem — always have the pre-eminence in this history, the ringleaders set at the head of the rest. Second, on the parenthesis about the doors: it is a note of historical accuracy, quietly signalling that what had earlier been said of setting up the doors of the gates in Nehemiah 3 was recorded there by way of anticipation, before the thing was actually done. The reformed John Gill simply marks that the wall was now quite finished, the breaches all made up.

Together the witnesses set the scene for the whole chapter: a great work all but complete, and a knot of frustrated enemies turning from force to fraud, resolved to accomplish by craft what they could not carry by arms. The very success of the building has raised the stakes; with the wall standing and only the doors to hang, the plotters have run out of time for a siege and must try, instead, to remove the one man on whom the enterprise depends.
2:
Twice foiled at the wall, the enemies now try to draw its builder away from it. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give the bare proposal — Sanballat and Geshem sent, saying, “Come, let us meet together in one of the villages in the plain of Ono” — and let the narrator’s own aside carry the menace: “but they thought to do me mischief.” The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke names that mischief plainly. They wished to get Nehemiah out of Jerusalem and away from his friends, that they might either carry him off or murder him; Ono, he notes, lay in the tribe of Benjamin, near the Jordan, a lonely enough spot for such a design.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads much from the very list of names. Tobiah, prominent in the previous verse, is here dropped, and is not distinguished by a preposition of his own; he appears now only as Sanballat’s secretary, the agent rather than the principal. As for the meeting-place, Ellicott fixes it at a particular village — Hakkephirim — in the plain of Ono, on the borders of Philistia, more than twenty miles from Jerusalem. The distance is itself the trap’s cunning: far enough that Nehemiah, once come down, would be well beyond the reach of rescue, and the plain a neutral ground where neither city’s guard could reach him.

The reformed John Gill adds that the summons came by messengers, so that the invitation was pressed with a show of formality, and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley supplies the plausible pretext under which it was framed — a meeting, they would have Nehemiah believe, to consult about the common service of their master the king of Persia, or to arrange some friendly accommodation between the provinces. The invitation wore the face of statecraft and neighbourliness; beneath it lay the intention to be rid of the governor by force or by blood.

Together the witnesses lay bare the anatomy of the plot. The offer is courteous, the place remote, the reasons politic; and the whole is aimed at separating Nehemiah from the city and the people who guarded him. Gill marks the messengers, Wesley the fair pretext, Clarke the deadly purpose, Ellicott the telling silence about Tobiah and the significant distance to Ono. What none of them lets the reader forget is the single clause with which Nehemiah unmasks the scheme before it is fairly begun — “but they thought to do me mischief.” The plain of Ono was to be no council-chamber but a snare, and the meeting a lure to draw the shepherd from the flock, so that the wall might be left, at the last, without its master.
3:
Nehemiah’s reply has become proverbial, and the witnesses weigh both its prudence and its dignity. The reformed John Gill observes the restraint of the manner: Nehemiah showed no open contempt of his enemies, nor even returned answer by their own messenger, but sent some of his own people to them — a measured, deliberate reply rather than a hot refusal. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke admires the discretion of its substance. Though Nehemiah knew their design well enough, he did not think it prudent to name it; had he charged them openly, they might have gone to extremities, and perhaps in a formidable body have fallen upon Jerusalem while it was ill provided to sustain the shock. They wished to gain their end by treachery rather than by open violence, and Nehemiah would not force their hand.

For Clarke the words themselves are a model for every busy servant of God: “I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down.” He knows no language more fitly used against the thousand invitations and provocations that would call a man from important labour to useless conference or to notice the malice of his detractors — “I am doing a great work, so I cannot stoop to your nonsense, or notice your malevolence. Why should the work cease, while I leave it, and come down to such as you?” The refusal is at once humble about the greatness of the task and lofty in its estimate of the triflers who would interrupt it.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the answer as heaven-taught wisdom. Nehemiah’s God, he says, instructed him to give this prudent reply by messengers of his own; his one care was that the work might not cease, for he knew that if he left it, even a little, it would stand still. He says nothing of his jealousies and reproaches them with no treachery, but gives a good and a true reason for staying. “Compliment,” Henry famously draws out, “must always give way to business”; let those who are tempted to idle, merry meetings by their vain companions answer the temptation as Nehemiah answered his enemies — “We have work to do, and must not neglect it.”

So the three witnesses converge on a single portrait of holy diligence. Gill fixes the calm, courteous form of the reply; Clarke its shrewd concealment of what Nehemiah knew and its universal application to every laborer beset by distractions; Henry its divine origin and its lesson that the work of God is never to be suspended for the sake of a conference with those who wish it ill. Between them they turn a single sentence of refusal into a rule for the whole of a diligent life — the building went on because its master would not be argued off the wall.
4:
The same invitation and the same refusal are repeated to the point of exhaustion, and the witnesses read the persistence on both sides. The reformed John Gill marks how eager the enemies were: four times they sent “after this sort,” being very pressing and importunate, so desirous were they of getting Nehemiah into their hands. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note the exact symmetry — they sent four times in the same manner, comparing the fixed phrase to the repeated overtures of 2 Samuel 15:6 — and Nehemiah gave them, each time, the very same answer.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley turns the repetition into a rule of conduct. We must never be overcome, he says, by the greatest importunity, to do anything ill or imprudent; but when we are attacked with the same temptation, we must still resist it with the same reason and the same resolution. The steadiness of Nehemiah is not stubbornness but principle: a good reason once given does not lose its force by being pressed against a fourth time, and the tempter who returns with the old bait deserves only the old refusal.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells on how galling that steadiness must have been to the plotters. Four times they attacked him with the same solicitation, and he as often returned the same answer — “I answered them after the same manner” — which, Henry supposes, was very vexatious to them; for it was in truth the ceasing of the work that they aimed at, and to see the undertaker so intent upon his undertaking made them despair of ever breaking it. Every fresh embassy that came back empty was a fresh proof that this man would not be moved. From it Henry draws the same note Wesley draws: we must never suffer ourselves to be overcome, by repeated urgency, to do anything sinful or imprudent, but when assailed by the same temptation must meet it with the same reason and resolution.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the enemies’ dogged eagerness, Keil and Delitzsch the formulaic sameness of the exchange, Wesley and Henry the settled constancy that made Nehemiah proof against it. Between them they show a contest of wills in which mere persistence, however patient, breaks upon a firmer patience; and they leave the reader with a maxim worth more than the incident — that the way to answer a temptation renewed is to renew, unshaken, the answer that first refused it. What wearied the enemies was not a new argument but an old one held fast.
5:
At the fifth attempt Sanballat drops his partners and his courtesy at once. The reformed John Gill notes that he now sent in his own name alone, neither Tobiah nor Geshem joining him, as though more anxious than any of them to get Nehemiah into his hands — perhaps, Gill suggests, affecting a warmer friendship than the rest, and writing privately as if the others knew nothing of it. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch record what changed: Sanballat sent his servant “with an open letter in his hand,” and the letter, for the first time, dropped the invitation and made an open charge, its contents recited in the verses that follow.

On that open letter the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fastens as a studied insult. Letters sent to chiefs and governors in the East, he explains, are always carefully folded, put into costly silken bags, and sealed; to send Nehemiah a missive unsealed and exposed was a deliberate mark of contempt for a man of his rank. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the openness of the letter to a further end, as speaking of a thing meant to seem commonly known — the accusation paraded as public rumour rather than as private malice.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott gathers both threads and adds the strategy behind the change. Four times, he recalls, the enemies had striven to induce Nehemiah to meet them under various pretexts, and each time his reply had been, in effect, that he was finishing his own work and could not come — an answer, Ellicott notes, not without a touch of irony, and one of universal application that preachers have long known how to use. Now the tactics shift. The silken bag containing the missive was deliberately left unsealed, in the hope that Nehemiah would be alarmed at the thought that its slanderous contents had already been read by the very people over whom he ruled.

The witnesses converge on the psychology of the move. Gill fixes Sanballat’s solitary eagerness and feigned friendship; Clarke the insult in the unsealed letter; Wesley the pretence that the thing was common talk; Ellicott the shift from enticement to intimidation and the hope of frightening Nehemiah with a slander seemingly public. The whole device is one of pressure by publicity: an unsealed charge is a charge already, in effect, broadcast, and Sanballat means the governor to feel the eyes of the province upon him before he has read a word. Where the earlier letters had whispered “come down and meet us,” this one shouts, and the change of key prepares the reader for the accusation the next verse sets down in full.
6:
The letter’s accusation is now set out, and the witnesses examine both its content and its craft. The reformed John Gill hears in “it is reported among the heathen” the pretence of a wide and public rumour: not a thing whispered among a few, but common talk in every mouth of the surrounding nations, noised abroad in divers lands. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch lay out the charge in full — that Nehemiah and the Jews thought to rebel, that for this cause he built the wall, and that he meant to be their king. Sanballat added, they note, that Nehemiah had appointed prophets to proclaim of him at Jerusalem, and closed with the veiled threat, “now shall it be reported to the king,” and the smooth proposal, “come now therefore, and let us take counsel together.” By flinging such accusations in an open letter that any might read, Sanballat thought to oblige Nehemiah to come and clear himself by an interview.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott savours the accuracy of the report. Nehemiah, he observes, can quote the very letter, preserving even its dialectal spelling — the “Gashmu” for Geshem first met at Nehemiah 2:19. He traces the argument’s cunning: Geshem is made to circulate a report which, reaching the distant Persian king, would be construed as rebellion; it is hinted that the heathen, the surrounding nations, would side with the king against Judah; and the words the true prophets had spoken concerning a future King are twisted into evidence of Nehemiah’s own ambition. Finally the letter suggests, with false friendliness, the desirableness of taking counsel together to avert the danger.

What the witnesses together expose is a slander built for maximum leverage. The rebellion is made to seem notorious abroad; the ambition is fathered on Nehemiah by a perversion of prophecy; the Persian court is invoked as the tribunal that will punish it; and the remedy offered is the very meeting Nehemiah has four times refused. Gill fixes the pretence of common report, Keil and Delitzsch the several strands of the charge and its aim of forcing a self-clearing interview, Ellicott the exactness of Nehemiah’s quotation and the political menace folded into it.

The accusation is designed to work three ways at once: either to hurry Nehemiah to court in his own defence, and so leave the wall; or to fright him from his labour altogether; or to bring him at last to the fatal parley at Ono. Every clause is aimed at motion — at getting the builder, by fear or by self-justification, to come down from his work. Against all three designs the following verses show him proof, meeting a manufactured rumour with a plain and fearless denial.
7:
The accusation sharpens to its most dangerous point — that Nehemiah had suborned prophets to proclaim him king — and the witnesses read the charge as a piece of transparent projection. The reformed John Gill sees Sanballat covering his own tracks: it was he and Tobiah who had been tampering with the prophets, corrupting and hiring them to discourage Nehemiah and bring the work to a stand; and now he lays that very crime at Nehemiah’s door, accusing him of appointing prophets to preach of him at Jerusalem. The slanderer paints his victim in the colours of his own guilt, and the charge is the more plausible because Sanballat knew from within how such prophets could be bought.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fills in the substance of the alleged proclamation — prophets set on to cry, in effect, “Nehemiah reigneth!” — and exposes the false warmth of the letter’s close. “Come now therefore, and let us take counsel together” means, Clarke says, come and justify yourself before me; and the whole was but a trick to get Nehemiah into Sanballat’s power. The offer of friendly consultation is the same snare as before, only baited now with the fear of a treason charge rather than the courtesy of a neighbourly meeting; the honey has changed, but the hook is unaltered.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley glosses the two clauses that carry the threat and the bait. “There is a king in Judah” he paraphrases as the rumour Sanballat pretends is abroad — “we have now a king of our own nation” — the very language of revolt from Persia, and the surest word to rouse a jealous court. And the invitation to take counsel he reads in Sanballat’s feigned voice: that we may impartially examine the matter, and that thy innocency may be cleared. The pretended aim is Nehemiah’s vindication; the real aim is his person.

Together the witnesses show the accusation for what it is: a charge manufactured out of the accuser’s own practices, dressed as concern, and pointed at the one meeting Nehemiah has steadily declined. Gill uncovers the projection — the hirer of prophets crying “hired prophets”; Clarke the demand that Nehemiah come and clear himself, which is really a demand that he deliver himself up; Wesley the double edge of “a king in Judah” and the counsel that offered clearance while it plotted capture. The letter’s friendliest phrase hides its deadliest intent, and Nehemiah, as the next verse shows, was not deceived by it for a moment.
8:
Nehemiah’s answer to the slander is flat, brief, and unafraid. The reformed John Gill notes only that he “sent unto him,” whether by letter or by messenger the text does not say, but the reply itself needs no elaboration: there are no such things done as thou sayest. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch weigh the second clause — “thou feignest them out of thine own heart” — and note that the verb rendered “feignest” comes from a root meaning to invent or fabricate, the same word used of Jeroboam devising a feast “out of his own heart” in 1 Kings 12:33. The word carries the flavour of malicious invention: the report is not merely mistaken but manufactured, spun deliberately out of Sanballat’s own imagination.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke admires the composure of the retort. “There are no such things done” says in effect, you well know that what you say is false; I shall not, therefore, trouble myself about a false charge. Nehemiah neither panics at the accusation nor dignifies it with a laboured defence. He does not hasten to Persia to clear himself, nor come down to Ono to argue the point, nor summon witnesses to disprove a rebellion that never was. He simply denies the thing and names its source — the accuser’s own heart.

The economy of the reply is itself instructive. A guilty man, or a frightened one, would have written pages; Nehemiah writes a sentence. He knows that the charge was framed not to be believed but to be used, a lever to pry him from his work or bring him to a fatal interview, and he refuses to grant it the weight of a long rebuttal. To feigned rumour he opposes plain contradiction; to manufactured slander, the calm assurance of a clear conscience. There is a strength in brevity here that a longer protest would have squandered, for the very length of a defence can lend a lie the dignity of a debate.

The witnesses converge without a seam. Gill fixes the bare fact of the reply; Keil and Delitzsch expose, in the very word for “feign,” that Nehemiah charged Sanballat not with error but with fabrication; Clarke commends the refusal to be troubled by what both parties knew to be false. The lesson they leave is that of the exemplary answer to calumny: deny it truly, trace it to its source, and return at once to the work — for the surest refutation of the lie that Nehemiah sought a crown was the wall he went on building for the people of God.
9:
Nehemiah lifts the veil on the enemies’ real aim, and then, in a single breath, turns from them to God. The reformed John Gill glosses “they all made us afraid” as pointing either to Sanballat and his circle or, with the older Jewish expositors, to all the surrounding heathen nations: the whole design of those scandalous reports was to intimidate the builders. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch put the purpose in the plotters’ own reasoning — they all desired to make us afraid, thinking, “their hands shall be weakened from the work, that it be not done.” The letters and the lures were never really about a meeting; they were about paralysis.

Then comes the abrupt cry, “Now therefore, O God, strengthen my hands.” Keil and Delitzsch explain the sudden shift by supposing that Nehemiah, writing afterward, is carried back into the very feelings of that hour, so that his narrative breaks into the prayer he then prayed; the word “strengthen” is an imperative addressed to God, and the ancient renderings that made it “I strengthened my hands” only reflect translators struggling to fit words they did not grasp. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads it likewise as one of the sudden, interjectional petitions that stud this book, remarkable here for its bareness — the words “O God,” supplied by the translators, are strictly an insertion, so that the prayer flashes out almost without naming the One to whom it flies.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley commends the petition as a pattern: a good prayer for us whenever we are entering upon any particular services or conflicts in our Christian warfare. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry expands it into a whole theology of dependence. It is the great support of good people, he says, that in all their straits they have a good God to go to, from whom by faith and prayer they may fetch in grace to silence their fears and strengthen their hands, just when their enemies are labouring to fill them with fears and weaken their hands. Some, Henry adds, read the clause not as a prayer but as a holy resolution — “now therefore I will strengthen my hands” — and either way the truth stands: Christian fortitude is sharpened by opposition, and every temptation that would draw us from duty should quicken us the more to it.

The witnesses agree on the whole movement. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch fix the enemies’ true object — not conference but the weakening of the workers’ hands; Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch the interjectional suddenness of the prayer; Wesley and Henry its exemplary force. The very stratagem meant to unnerve Nehemiah becomes the occasion of his turning to God for the strength his enemies hoped to steal, so that their intimidation recoils into his intercession.
10:
The assault changes shape a third time, from enticement and slander to a plot dressed in the robes of prophecy. The reformed John Gill introduces the actor: Shemaiah the son of Delaiah, the son of Mehetabeel, “who was shut up” — confined in his own house or a temple chamber, as though wholly given to meditation, fasting, and prayer. He may have been a priest of the course of Delaiah, and Nehemiah, holding him in good esteem, came to his house to consult him. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the seclusion the same way, as a pretence of singular devotion and of certain knowledge, gained by the Spirit of God, concerning an approaching danger from which safety could be found nowhere but in the temple.

The grammatical-historical witnesses expose the design. Keil and Delitzsch identify Shemaiah as a false prophet hired by Tobiah and Sanballat, who by predicting that Nehemiah’s enemies would kill him in the night sought to drive him to flee into the holy place and bar the doors — the aim being, as Nehemiah later saw, to lure him into an illegal act that would furnish occasion to speak evil of him. Charles Ellicott adds that Shemaiah, probably a priest, was found shut up in his house, represented himself as endangered by the common enemy, foretold a nocturnal attempt on Nehemiah’s life, and proposed that they meet “within the Temple” — in the holy place, between the Holiest and the outer court — for security.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws out the ruin the counsel would have worked. “Shut yourself up in the temple,” it urged in effect, “for there alone is safety”; but had Nehemiah done so, the people would have been left without their leader, an easy prey to the enemy, his government would have seemed at an end, and Sanballat might have seized the reins. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry names the deeper strategy: the enemies, having failed to fetch Nehemiah out of the country, now try to drive him into hiding — anywhere but at his work. Observing him to be a cautious man, they hope to conquer him through his very caution, tempting him to a foolish flight that they might reproach him for it.

Henry adds the sting of the deception: the tools were a pretended prophet and, with the prophetess Noadiah, a pretended prophetess, hired to persuade Nehemiah to quit his post; and the pretext was plausible, for the enemies really would have slain him if they could. It was, Henry says, the devil’s own work, to draw a man into sin under the colour of religion — and no temptation comes with more force than one that wears the dress of revelation and devotion and is brought by the hand of a prophet, urging even the shelter of the sanctuary, as the psalmist speaks of God hiding his own in his pavilion in Psalms 27:5. Self-preservation, Henry warns, is a first law of nature, yet the counsel that pleads it is not always the wisest.
11:
Nehemiah’s refusal to hide breaks out in a question that is half rebuke, half creed. The reformed John Gill hears in “should such a man as I flee?” the voice of the king’s commissioner, on whom the whole enterprise depended — for if he absented himself the people would scatter and the wall be left defenceless, which was the very thing the plotters hoped for; and this was the man who had so signally professed his confidence in God and seen it honoured with success. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke amplifies the office: shall I, who am governor, appointed by both God and the king, betray my trust and leave the flock without a shepherd? I will stand at my post, and be ready to receive my enemies whenever they come.

The grammatical-historical witnesses probe the second, harder clause — “who is there, that, being as I am, would go into the temple to save his life?” Keil and Delitzsch note the ambiguity of the closing word: it may mean “to save his life,” or it may mean the opposite, that one so entering could not thereby live but would rather expiate the trespass with his life, since the law of Numbers 18:7 ordained that the stranger who came near the holy things should be put to death. Charles Ellicott divides the sentence into its two motives: first personal dignity — should such a man as I flee? — then a scruple of fear, “who, being as I am,” a layman, “would go into the Temple” and, on the better rendering, “live?” For Nehemiah to save his life by so entering would be to forfeit it under that same law.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley gathers the reasons into one impassioned refusal. “As I” — the chief governor, upon whose presence the very life of the whole city and nation in great measure depended; who had professed such resolution and courage and confidence in God; who had known such eminent experience of God’s help in dangers greater than this. Shall I now dishonour God and religion, and betray the people and city of God, by my cowardice? And so his resolve stands flat against the prophet’s counsel: “I will not go in” — though, Wesley adds, his very life had seemed to hang upon it.

The witnesses converge on a double ground of refusal. Gill, Clarke, and Wesley press the argument from station: a leader may not flee where his flight would ruin those he leads, for the courage of the head is the courage of the whole body. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott press the argument from law: a layman may not save himself by a trespass that would cost his life and profane the house of God. Between honour and holiness Nehemiah has no room to flee, and knows it — the very fear the prophet meant to plant becomes the occasion of his firmest stand.
12:
Behind the pious counsel Nehemiah discerns a hired hand, and the witnesses trace how he came to see it. The reformed John Gill gives the plainest test: Nehemiah perceived that God had not sent Shemaiah, because the man advised what was against the cause of God and true religion. A prophet urging an act that would desecrate the temple and desert the work could not be speaking from God, whatever his pretensions; the counsel condemned the counsellor, and the message betrayed the messenger.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch add the precise ground and the grammar of Nehemiah’s insight. He perceived it, they note, from Shemaiah’s own conduct once his advice was refused; the false prophet’s manner, when his scheme failed, gave him away. And the Hebrew throws the emphasis hard upon the denial — “not God had sent him,” the negative standing pointedly before the divine name, as if to say it was anyone but God who inspired these words. Shemaiah had pronounced this prophecy against Nehemiah not because heaven had commissioned him, but because Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him, the singular verb of hiring fastening chiefly on the ringleader while embracing both conspirators.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells on the discernment itself and its lesson. “I perceived that God had not sent him” — that he gave this advice not by any divine direction, ordinary or extraordinary, but with a design against Nehemiah. The wickedness of such mercenary wretches, Henry observes, will sooner or later be brought to light; the man who lets himself be bought to betray a good cause under the mask of prophecy cannot forever hide the hire that moves him. Nehemiah’s spiritual instinct, sharpened by his knowledge of the law and his sense of the work God had given him, cut through the disguise at once, and would not be overawed by a prophet’s claim.

The witnesses do not divide; they build one lesson in the discernment of spirits. Gill supplies the doctrinal criterion — a message that contradicts the cause of God is not from God; Keil and Delitzsch the circumstantial evidence — Shemaiah’s behaviour betrayed him, and the emphatic Hebrew underscores that God had no part in it; Henry the moral certainty that hired treachery will out. A false prophet is unmasked not by louder claims to inspiration but by the tendency of his counsel; and Nehemiah, weighing the advice against the known will of God, knew a bought man when he heard one.
13:
The purpose behind the hire is now laid open, and the witnesses trace the chain from bribe to intended ruin. The reformed John Gill marks the plain statement of the design — “therefore was he hired, that I should be afraid, and do so” — the fear meant to produce the act, and the act to produce the fall. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch unfold the sequence, noting the peculiar Hebrew that strings one purpose upon another: for this end was Shemaiah hired, that Nehemiah might be frightened, and act on his fear, and sin; and had he sinned by entering and shutting himself within the holy place, that trespass would have become to his enemies matter for an evil report, a handle by which to defame him. To take refuge in the sanctuary as a layman would have been a grave desecration of the house of God, the very thing to cast suspicion on Nehemiah as a despiser of God’s commands and so undermine his authority with the people.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott states it in a sentence: Nehemiah perceived that not God but Shemaiah himself had uttered the prophecy against him, and that the prophet was hired to bring the governor into discredit as a violator of the law. The whole plot, in this reading, aimed not at Nehemiah’s body but at his reputation — to make the guardian of the law appear its transgressor, and so to turn the people’s reverence for the temple against the man who would not profane it.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley spells out both halves of the snare. “And sin” means by going into a place forbidden to him, and in such a manner as would have been at once sinful and shameful; “that they might reproach me” means that they might brand him a coward, conscious of his own guilt, and so make him contemptible and odious both to his own people and to the king of Persia. The two ruins, spiritual and political, were bound together: the same act that offended God would have disgraced the governor.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the two dreads Nehemiah felt: the fear of offending God — “that I should be afraid, and do so, and sin” — and the fear of shaming himself — “that they might reproach me.” Sin, Henry says, is what above anything we should dread; and a good preservative against it is to fear nothing but sin. Next to the sinfulness of sin we should dread the scandalousness of it, and Nehemiah, weighing both, would neither transgress the law nor hand his enemies the slander they had paid so dearly to obtain.
14:
The account of the plots closes on a prayer, and the witnesses weigh both its object and its restraint. The reformed John Gill reads “my God, think thou on Tobiah and Sanballat according to these their works” as a plea that God would not merely confound and disappoint their wicked schemes but reward the plotters as they deserved. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that with the two chief enemies Nehemiah names also the prophetess Noadiah and the rest of the prophets who, like Shemaiah, would have put him in fear — the whole hireling company gathered under one petition, so that none of the confederacy is forgotten before God.

On the name Noadiah the witnesses divide. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke doubts the reading: whether this was a prophet or prophetess is uncertain; the Hebrew text makes the person a prophetess, yet the ancient versions render “Noadiah the prophet,” and Clarke judges that the feminine ending is a scribal mistake and that we should read “the prophet.” The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, by contrast, takes the prophetess at face value and finds in her very obscurity an argument for the record’s truth: the mention of a name that occurs nowhere else shows the circumstantial, particular character of the narrative and is an indirect evidence of its authenticity. Keil and Delitzsch and Gill likewise read her as a real woman among the false prophets, so that the sole question is whether the text should stand as a prophetess or be emended to a prophet.

Ellicott frames the prayer itself as an official prophetic petition: Nehemiah puts God’s own cause into God’s own hands. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry guards it from any charge of vindictiveness. As, when Nehemiah had rehearsed his own good services, he did not prescribe his reward but modestly prayed, “think upon me, my God,” at Nehemiah 5:19, so here he does not imprecate any particular judgment upon his enemies but refers the whole matter to God: thou knowest their hearts, and art the avenger of falsehood and wrong; judge between me and them.

Whatever injuries are done us, Henry concludes, we must not avenge ourselves, but commit our cause to him that judgeth righteously. The witnesses leave Nehemiah where the godly always leave their enemies — in the hands of God — asking not that he might strike them himself, but that the righteous Judge would weigh their works and answer their malice in his own time and way.
15:
Against every plot the work is simply, triumphantly finished. The reformed John Gill dates it exactly: the wall was completed on the twenty-fifth day of the month Elul, the sixth month, answering to part of August and part of September — a note the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley echoes, Elul answering partly to our August and partly to September. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry seizes on the fifty-two days and their meaning. The adversaries had the mortification to see the wall built despite all their attempts; it was begun and finished in fifty-two days, and yet, he reckons, they rested on the sabbaths. Many hands were employed and there was room for them; what they did they did cheerfully, minding their business because they loved it; and the very threats meant to weaken them served rather to quicken them, that they might finish before the enemy came. Thus, Henry says, out of the eater came forth meat — borrowing Samson’s riddle in Judges 14:14 — and we see what a deal of work may be done in a little time if we set about it in earnest and keep close to it.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke defends the short span against all incredulity. He sees no difficulty in supposing that several thousand workmen, each labouring as for God, should finish in fifty-two days; much of the old wall stood entire, its foundations largely remained, the materials lay at hand, and they had rubbish to clear but no stone to quarry. He sets the feat beside greater ones — Caesar’s works in Gaul, Titus raising a wall about Jerusalem in three days, Alexander building the walls of Alexandria in some twenty to thirty days — so that Nehemiah had time enough and to spare.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott agrees, dating the twenty-fifth of Elul to about our fifteenth of September and the beginning of the work to the latter part of July. Given that the wall was only partially overthrown, the materials ready, and the bands of workmen organized with the utmost skill, the time is not too short, and there is no need of the two years and four months Josephus imagined.

Above all Ellicott hears the theology of the closing clause: that the enemies perceived the work “wrought of our God” means not that it was miraculous but that it was done under the divine sanction and help — and by that confession Nehemiah at once triumphs over his foes and gives the glory where it is due, his own heroic part in the labour utterly forgotten. The witnesses converge on a single wonder: a wall that months of intrigue could not stop was raised in fifty-two days, and its very speed became the plainest signature of God upon the work.
16:
The finished wall does to the enemies’ spirits what no argument could: it casts them down. The reformed John Gill notes simply that all the adversaries heard the wall was finished; the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch draw out the effect. The news spread fear among the surrounding nations — the neighbours already glimpsed at Nehemiah 4:1 — who were “much cast down in their own eyes,” for they perceived that the work was effected with the help of Israel’s God. The idiom, they observe, occurs only here, and is to be understood after the manner of the countenance that “fell” in Genesis 4:5 and the heart, that is the courage, that “fails” in 1 Samuel 17:32: they sank in their own esteem, felt themselves cast down and discouraged.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the clause “this work was wrought of our God” as an added reason not to wonder at the short time in which so great a thing was done: God helped the builders by an especial providence, and that providence was so plain that even their carnal enemies could discern it. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott puts the whole verse in a line — the enemies heard of it, saw the result, and were ashamed.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the several strands of their dismay. They were ashamed of their own confident boast that they should cause the work to cease, and now stood crest-fallen at the disappointment; they envied the prosperity and success of the Jews; and they despaired at last of doing them the mischief they had designed, perceiving by the wonderful speed that the work was of God. Even these heathen, Henry marvels, had sense enough to see a special providence at work in the affairs of the church when it visibly prospered — to say, as the psalmist puts it, “the Lord hath done great things for them” in Psalms 126:2 — to believe that God’s work would be perfect, and to conclude that if the thing were of God it was to no purpose to oppose it.

The witnesses converge on a single reversal. Gill fixes the report, Keil and Delitzsch the sunken hearts and the vivid idiom of a fallen countenance, Clarke the providence so patent that enemies confessed it, Ellicott the shame, Henry the mingled envy and despair. The wall that the plotters had laboured to prevent became, once standing, the most eloquent of witnesses — forcing from the mouths of pagans the very acknowledgment they had least wished to make, that God himself had built it.
17:
The finished wall did not finish Nehemiah’s troubles; a treachery within now comes to light. The reformed John Gill sets the note in time — “in those days,” while the wall was building — and the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read it as a supplementary remark Nehemiah adds: in those days even the nobles of Judah were in active correspondence with Tobiah, multiplying their letters to him and receiving his in return, because he had married into a respectable Jewish family. The plain sense is startling: the leading men of the community were exchanging a busy correspondence with one of its chief enemies, and the very ink that should have served the city was carrying its counsels out to Ammon.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws out how much this deepened Nehemiah’s difficulty. He had enemies without and false friends within; a treacherous correspondence ran between the nobles of Judah and the Ammonite Tobiah, and, Clarke judges, had almost any other man than Nehemiah been at the head of Jewish affairs, Jerusalem would never have been re-established. The peril of the traitor at the council table is greater than that of the foe at the gate, for the one may be watched and the other cannot. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott simply confirms the scale of it — there was a large correspondence between Tobiah and the nobles of Judah, no occasional note but a steady traffic.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry feels the shame of it keenly. Even of the nobles of Judah there were those who had so little sense of honour and of their country’s good as to keep up a familiar correspondence with Tobiah, writing to him and welcoming his letters. Could nobles do a thing so mean? Nobles of Judah so wicked a thing? It seems, Henry reflects, that great men are not always wise, and not always honest; rank is no guarantee of loyalty, and the highest seats in a community may harbour its most damaging disloyalty.

The witnesses agree in reading the verse as a portrait of danger from within. Gill fixes the time, Keil and Delitzsch the marriage-tie that bound the nobles to Tobiah, Clarke the peculiar peril of false friends at home, Ellicott the sheer volume of the traffic, Henry the disgrace that men of honour should stoop to it. The wall could be built against foes outside; but a leader whose own nobility trafficked with the enemy carried a breach in his defences that no masonry could close, and the next verses will show how that breach had been opened.
18:
The root of the nobles’ treachery was a web of marriage and oath, and the witnesses trace its threads. The reformed John Gill notes that many in Judah were “sworn unto him” — bound to Tobiah not only by private correspondence but by an oath to be true to his interest and to act as he should advise them. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch explain that Tobiah was connected with two Jewish families: he was son-in-law of Shecaniah the son of Arah, a respectable Jew of the race of Arah named in Ezra 2:5, and his son Johanan had married the daughter of Meshullam the son of Berechiah, who appears among the builders of the wall at Nehemiah 3:4. From this they infer that the many bound to Tobiah were “associates of an oath,” joined to him by a sworn compact rather than a mere treaty, and that his affinity by marriage was itself confirmed with an oath. They add that even the high priest Eliashib was related to him, as Nehemiah 13:4 records, while the genuinely Hebrew names of both Tobiah and his son suggest how readily such affinities were formed.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets the same connections in order: Shecaniah of the family of Arah had come up with Zerubbabel; Tobiah married his daughter, and Tobiah’s son married a daughter of Meshullam the builder — and this family connection ripened into a conspiracy by oath to thwart the governor. The Hebrew names, Ellicott suggests, point to Tobiah and his son being naturalised Ammonites of Hebrew extraction, which makes the readiness of the intermarriage the easier to understand.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke widens the lens to the whole disease of mixed marriage. Before Nehemiah’s coming the Jews had been fast intermixing with the heathen — with Ashdodites, Ammonites, and Moabites, as Nehemiah 13:23 laments, and as Ezra had already laboured to redress among priests and chiefs in Ezra 9:3. But here, Clarke observes, the heathen and the Jewish nobles are actually interlinked, the nobility so far imbued with the spirit of idolatry that they forgot God, his service, their brethren, and their own souls.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the moral in a phrase. See, he says, the mischief of marrying with strangers: when men once became akin to Tobiah, they soon became sworn to him, for a sinful love leads to a sinful league. The witnesses converge on one lesson — that the breach in Nehemiah’s defences had been opened long before, in the marriage-beds of Judah’s great houses, and that the oaths which now bound the nobles to an enemy were the ripened fruit of alliances the law had forbidden.
19:
The chapter ends with the nobles playing a double game, and the witnesses expose both faces of it. The reformed John Gill notes how they spoke of Tobiah to Nehemiah: they reported his good deeds before the governor, recommending him as a worthy man deserving of respect and friendship, whose counsel and acquaintance might be of service. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set beside this the other direction of their talk — “they uttered my words to him,” carrying Nehemiah’s sayings back to Tobiah. The subject throughout is the nobles of Judah, praising Tobiah’s good qualities to Nehemiah while reporting Nehemiah’s words to Tobiah; and though, as Keil and Delitzsch grant with Bertheau, there is no need to suppose they distorted his words to widen the breach, by this very traffic they were playing straight into Tobiah’s hands, so that at the last “Tobiah sent letters to put me in fear.”

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott joins the two motions into one intelligence system. Besides the correspondence already noted, these nobles strove to exalt the character of Tobiah before the governor, while at the same time making the enemy acquainted with all that went on; and it was this steady flow of intelligence that enabled Tobiah to write the disquieting letters Nehemiah was continually receiving. Every word carried in and every report carried out fed the same campaign of intimidation, so that the praise and the espionage were two hands of one design.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks the effrontery of it. They had the impudence to court Nehemiah himself into a friendship with Tobiah, reporting his good deeds and pressing him as a man worth confiding in. We are indeed required to speak ill of no man, Henry allows, but never to speak well of bad men; those that forsake the law praise the wicked, as Proverbs 28:4 warns. And they were false enough to betray Nehemiah’s counsels, uttering his words to Tobiah, no doubt with such misconstruction as furnished fresh matter for the frightening letters.

Thus, Henry concludes, were all their thoughts against Nehemiah for evil — yet God thought upon him for good. The witnesses close the chapter on that tension. Gill and Ellicott fix the two-way treachery — Tobiah praised to Nehemiah, Nehemiah reported to Tobiah; Keil and Delitzsch caution that the nobles need not have twisted his words to do him harm; Henry lays bare the impudence of praising a bad man and betraying a good one, and lifts the whole to its resolution. Against a wall of intrigue as real as the wall of stone, Nehemiah stood, encircled by letters meant to make him afraid — and behind him stood the God whose thoughts toward him were for good.
